newsitem.title: USA: Wachovia sees dilution, charges from deal.
newsitem.headline: Wachovia sees dilution, charges from deal.

text.p: Wachovia Corp said its proposed $2.3 billion acquisition of Central Fidelity Banks Inc would dilute earnings by 13.5 percent in 1997 and 4.0 to 4.5 percent in 1998.
In a conference call with reporters, chief financial officer Robert McCoy also said the deal was expected to be accretive to earnings by four percent in 1999.

McCoy also said Wachovia expects to take a charge of $136 million in 1997 related to the Central Fidelity deal, announced today, and its recently announced $542 million deal to buy Jefferson Bankshares Inc.
The timing of the charges was not immediately known.
In 1998, the company plans to take a $54 million charge related to the Central Fidelity deal, he said.

Wachovia Chief Executive Bud Baker said the company anticipates $79 million in cost savings from the acquisition. He said the deal is likely to result in overlap in some areas, but declined to estimate potential job losses.
A Wachovia spokesman subsequently told Reuters the bulk of the charges will be taken by the end of the second quarter of 1998.
Wachovia still sees opportunities for growth in Virginia, especially in the northern section of the state.
"North Virginia is clearly an area where we can look for some strenghening," Baker said.
Three members of the Central Fidelity board will be invited to join the Wachovia board, Baker said.
Shares of Wachovia, which initially rose after the deal was announced, slid 1-1/8 to 61-1/2 by early afternoon.
Central Fidelity chairman Lewis Miller said he approached Wachovia about a transaction after the company announced its June 10 deal with Jefferson Bankshares.

"Given Wachovia's size, it is able to invest heavily in technology. Technological advances are taking place in our industry at an amazing rate, and the investment to keep pace with this change is enormous," he said.

Baker said the transaction is expected to generate $10 million in potential revenue enhancements. Half of the anticipated cost savings and revenue enhancements will come next year, with the balance coming in 1999, he said.
